teaser: An army of skeletons takes a whole country, and Bruegel offers no way out.
review_notes:
The image file is small (960 px wide): interactive spots are limited to large, clearly readable groups.
The panel is neither signed nor dated; about 1562 (Prado: 1562 to 1563) is the usual dating. Lesson follows the catalog year and says 'around'.
The story of the servant girl and the notched stick comes from Karel van Mander (1604) and is presented as his story.
A link with the Triumph of Death fresco in Palermo is a hypothesis, presented as such.
Recorded in 1745 at La Granja among Queen Elisabeth Farnese's pictures; in the Prado since 1827; restored 2018.
The skeleton making music behind the lovers at far right is hard to make out at this resolution; described as 'behind them'.

lesson.text: Around 1562 Pieter Bruegel was in his mid-thirties, unmarried, and living in Antwerp. He earned his keep drawing designs for a print publisher: comic monsters, landscapes, moral scenes sold cheaply by the sheet. Within a year he would move to Brussels and marry Mayken Coecke, the daughter of his old teacher.

An early biographer, Karel van Mander, gives the move a romantic twist. In Antwerp, he says, Bruegel lived with a servant girl he would have married, except that she lied constantly. He cut a notch in a stick for each lie, and the stick filled up. His future mother-in-law insisted he leave the city.

In those last Antwerp months he painted his three darkest panels, all crawling with nightmare creatures. This is the bleakest. The city around him was rich and nervous: ruled from Spain, shaken by religious quarrels, used to public executions and to plague returning every few years.

The panel is about 117 by 162 cm (46 by 64 inches). The earth is scorched brown, the sky is smoke, ships burn on the sea. Across this land comes an army of skeletons, and the living, from top to bottom of society, have nowhere to go.

lesson.title: No one is spared
lesson.text: Read the foreground from left to right: Death takes each rank in turn.

spots.title: The king
spots.text: In crown, armor and ermine cloak, he has fallen. A skeleton shows him an hourglass: his time is up. Beside him another skeleton, in armor, helps itself to barrels of gold coins.

spots.title: The cart
spots.text: A wagon heaped with skulls is pulled by a starved horse. The skeleton riding on it turns a hurdy-gurdy, a cranked string instrument. Death arrives with music.

spots.title: The rider
spots.text: In the middle of the crush, a skeleton on a bony reddish horse swings a scythe. He drives the crowd to the right like cattle.

spots.title: The trap
spots.text: The crowd is herded into a huge box with a raised door. Ranks of skeletons stand guard behind coffin lids used as shields, each marked with a cross.

lesson.text: Two older traditions meet here. In Italy, where Bruegel traveled in the early 1550s, painters showed the Triumph of Death: Death as a rider mowing people down. He may have seen a famous example in Palermo. In the north, artists drew the Dance of Death: a skeleton leading away each social rank, pope to peasant, one by one.
Bruegel fuses the Italian rider and the northern dance into a war. What makes the picture so hard is what he leaves out: no angels, no judgment, no heaven. The only crosses belong to the enemy.

The tall poles topped with cartwheels on the horizon were not invented horrors. They were a real punishment of the time: the bodies of the executed were displayed on wheels raised in the air outside towns. Bruegel's viewers knew them by sight.
Yet the painter of village feasts is still here. In the bottom right corner a dinner party has just been interrupted, and a few guests have not understood yet.
While the world ends, two people are still making music. Find the lovers with the lute.

spots.title: The lovers
spots.text: In the bottom right corner a man plays the lute for a lady with a songbook. They have eyes only for each other. Behind them, Death has already joined in.

lesson.text: Beside the couple, the others react the way people do. A gentleman in a striped tunic draws his sword at an enemy no sword can hurt. A jester in checkered clothes dives under the tablecloth. Cards and a backgammon board lie spilled on the grass. Each response is useless, and each is very human.

spots.title: The table
spots.text: White cloth, plates, playing cards. A skeleton has seized a woman in a dance, while the man in red reaches for his sword.

spots.title: Fool and games
spots.text: The jester in red and white checks crawls for cover. Next to him lie a backgammon board and scattered cards: pleasure, luck and laughter are no defense.

spots.title: The bells
spots.text: At top left, skeletons haul on the ropes of two bells hung in a dead tree. They are tolling for everybody at once.

spots.title: White robes
spots.text: Skeletons draped in white, like a choir or a court, crowd a platform by the water and sound trumpets.

spots.title: The execution
spots.text: On the hill at top right, a kneeling man with bound eyes waits under a raised sword. Near him stand a gallows and the wheels on poles.

spots.title: Fire and wrecks
spots.text: Along the horizon, ships sink and fires burn. The destruction reaches as far as you can see.

lesson.text: The panel carries no signature and no date, and nobody knows who wanted such a thing on a wall. By 1745 it belonged to the queen of Spain, Elisabeth Farnese, at her palace of La Granja. It has hung in the Prado in Madrid since 1827.

Bruegel left Antwerp soon after. In Brussels his subjects turned to seasons, harvests and weddings. He never painted anything this hopeless again, though the knowledge behind it stays in the later pictures: the feasts are short, and the people in them seem to know it.

In 2018 the Prado cleaned the painting and removed old repaints and yellowed varnish. The dull brown that people had long taken for Bruegel's intention gave way to cooler blues and sharper reds, and many small figures became readable again.

quiz.question: How was Bruegel making his living in Antwerp around 1562?
options: As a court painter to the king of Spain
quiz.explanation: He drew designs that a publisher sold as cheap prints.

quiz.question: Which two traditions does the painting combine?
options: The Italian Triumph of Death and the northern Dance of Death
quiz.explanation: He fused Death as a rider with the dance that takes every rank.

quiz.question: What does the skeleton show the fallen king?
quiz.explanation: The hourglass tells him his time has run out.

quiz.question: What is missing from this vision of the end, compared with most religious art?
options: Any sign of heaven, angels or judgment
quiz.explanation: Bruegel offers no rescue; the only crosses are on the skeletons' shields.

quiz.question: What are the lovers in the bottom right corner doing?
quiz.explanation: He plays the lute for her, unaware of Death behind them.

facts.text: The painting is clearly signed and dated by Bruegel.
facts.explanation: It carries neither a signature nor a date.

facts.text: The wheels on poles show a real punishment of Bruegel's time.
facts.explanation: Bodies of the executed were displayed on raised wheels outside towns.

facts.text: Only the poor are attacked by the skeletons.
facts.explanation: Death takes every rank, starting with a king.
